title: Poor School Performance
overview: Poor academic performance is common and nonspecific. Most childhood mental disorders can impair it, and it is frequently the chief complaint — but it is not itself a disorder. Evaluation typically pairs cognitive/achievement testing with a careful history from parents, teachers, and clinicians. Because neurodevelopmental and other disorders often co-occur, traverse the tree more than once and assign every applicable diagnosis.

nodes.question: Are there deficits in intellectual function plus deficits in adaptive functioning, with onset during the developmental period?
Are there deficits in the social use of verbal and nonverbal communication?
nodes.note: If accompanied by restricted/repetitive behavior and deficits in relationships and social-emotional reciprocity, consider Autism Spectrum Disorder; otherwise Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder.

nodes.question: Are there also restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior/interests and deficits in developing/understanding relationships?

no.outcome: Social (Pragmatic) Communication Disorder

nodes.question: Is there difficulty learning and using specific academic skills (reading, writing, mathematics)?
Are there persistent difficulties in the acquisition and use of language?
Is there failure to speak in school despite speaking in other settings (e.g., home)?
Are there symptoms of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, onset before age 12, interfering with functioning across settings?
Is there a pattern of severe temper outbursts out of proportion to the situation with persistent anger/irritability between outbursts?
Is there a pattern of antisocial behavior (e.g., truancy, rule violations)?
Is there a pattern of negativistic, hostile, and defiant behavior?
Is the poor performance related to excessive substance use?
Is there school refusal based on fear of separation from attachment figures?
Is another anxiety, mood, or psychotic disorder interfering with school performance?
Is it a maladaptive response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor?

no.outcome: Not attributable to a mental disorder (e.g., poor work habits, disruptive environment, lack of motivation)

title: Behavioral Problems in a Child or Adolescent
presenting: Behavioral problems in a child or adolescent
overview: Many behavioral problems in youth are not due to a mental disorder — some are subthreshold, some reflect family dysfunction, and some serious acts (e.g., for financial gain) fall outside DSM-5. Early-childhood onset points toward ADHD, ODD, DMDD, ASD, or intellectual disability; adolescent onset raises the role of substances and adolescent-onset conduct disorder, mood disorders, and psychosis.

nodes.question: Are the behaviors associated with substance use (including medication)?
Are they due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition?

diagnoses.name: Delirium Due to Another Medical Condition
Major/Mild Neurocognitive Disorder, with Behavioral Disturbance
Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Do severe temper outbursts occur that are grossly out of proportion, with persistent anger/irritability between them?
Is there a persistent pattern of hyperactivity, impulsivity, and inattention across two or more settings with onset before age 12?
Is there a pattern of argumentativeness, defiance, and vindictiveness beyond developmental norms?
Do the behaviors occur with intellectual and adaptive deficits with onset in the developmental period?
Do they occur with persistent deficits in social communication/interaction plus restricted, repetitive behaviors?
Are they a consequence of stereotyped, repetitive motor movements?
Are they part of a repetitive, persistent pattern of antisocial behavior violating others' rights or major norms?
Is there deliberate, purposeful fire setting associated with arousal/fascination?
Is there recurrent failure to resist impulses to steal objects not needed for use or monetary value?
Are the behaviors associated with periods of elevated, euphoric, or irritable mood plus increased energy?
Are they associated with episodes of depressed/irritable mood plus other depressive symptoms?
Are they associated with psychotic symptoms?
Do the problems occur as a symptomatic response to a psychosocial stressor of an extremely traumatic nature, with re-experiencing?

diagnoses.name: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder / Acute Stress Disorder

nodes.question: Are they a maladaptive response to a (non-traumatic) psychosocial stressor?
Are the problems clinically significant and representative of a psychological/biological dysfunction, but not covered above?

diagnoses.name: Other Specified / Unspecified Disruptive, Impulse-Control, and Conduct Disorder

nodes.question: Is the behavior illegal behavior for gain or revenge (not a dysfunction in the individual)?

yes.outcome: Child or Adolescent Antisocial Behavior (V/Z code)

no.outcome: Age-appropriate rambunctious behavior — not a mental disorder

title: Speech Disturbance
overview: Covers disorganized speech (derailment, tangentiality), impaired speech production (language, articulation, fluency), and unusual speech (pragmatic deficits, pressured/repetitive speech). Disorganized speech is hard to judge — if you cannot readily tell whether speech is disorganized, it probably is not pathological. Distinguishing loosening of associations (schizophrenia) from flight of ideas (mania) is best based on accompanying symptoms and course rather than the speech pattern alone.

nodes.question: Is the speech disturbance associated with a fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness?
Is it associated with decline in one or more cognitive domains (attention, executive function, memory, language, perceptual-motor, social cognition)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a substance (including medication)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition (e.g., aphasia)?

diagnoses.name: Speech disturbance due to another medical condition (e.g., aphasia)

nodes.question: Is there rapid, pressured speech with racing thoughts, euphoric/irritable mood, and increased energy?
Is speech disorganized (derailment, incoherence) in the context of other psychotic symptoms?
Are there persistent difficulties in the acquisition and use of language?
Are there difficulties with speech sound production that reduce intelligibility?
Are there disturbances in fluency and time patterning of speech inappropriate for age?
Are there deficits in the social (pragmatic) use of verbal and nonverbal communication?
Are there inappropriate vocal outbursts in the context of otherwise normal speech?

no.outcome: Consider residual category or no mental disorder

title: Distractibility
overview: Reduced ability to sustain attention is nonspecific and occurs across many disorders. Rule out substances and medical causes, then distinguish attentional problems that are episodic and mood-linked (mania, depression, anxiety, psychosis) from the persistent, cross-situational, early-onset pattern of ADHD.

nodes.question: Is the distractibility due to the physiological effects of a substance (including medication)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition (including delirium)?
Does it occur only during periods of elevated, expansive, or irritable mood with increased energy?
Does it occur only during a Major Depressive Episode?
Does it occur only in the context of prominent anxiety or worry?
Does it occur only in the context of psychotic symptoms?
Is there a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity, onset before age 12, impairing across settings?
Are there persistent deficits in social communication and restricted/repetitive behaviors (ASD)?

no.outcome: Distractibility not attributable to a specific mental disorder (or subthreshold) — consider context

title: Delusions
overview: First confirm the belief is a true delusion and not a culturally or religiously sanctioned belief. Then apply the etiologic rule-outs (substance, medical) before differentiating among the primary psychotic and mood disorders. The mood/psychosis relationship — whether delusions are confined to mood episodes, and the proportion of the illness occupied by mood episodes — drives the schizophrenia vs. schizoaffective vs. mood-disorder-with-psychotic-features distinctions.

nodes.question: Is the belief a manifestation of a culturally or religiously sanctioned belief system?

yes.outcome: Not a delusion — no diagnosis on this basis

nodes.question: Are the delusions due to the physiological effects of a substance (including medication)?
Are they due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition?

yes.outcome: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Do the delusions occur exclusively during episodes of elevated/expansive/irritable mood?

diagnoses.name: Bipolar I/II Disorder, With Psychotic Features

nodes.question: Do the delusions occur exclusively during Major Depressive Episodes?

diagnoses.name: Major Depressive Disorder, With Psychotic Features

nodes.question: Have the delusions (with other active-phase symptoms) persisted for 6 months or more?
nodes.note: Duration and the mood relationship separate schizophrenia, schizophreniform, schizoaffective, brief psychotic, and delusional disorder.

nodes.question: Are the delusions accompanied by other characteristic psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, or negative symptoms)?

no.outcome: Delusional Disorder

nodes.question: Is there a history of Major Depressive or Manic Episodes overlapping the active psychotic period?

no.outcome: Schizophrenia

nodes.question: Have mood episodes been present for the MAJORITY of the total active/residual illness, AND were there ≥2 weeks of delusions/hallucinations without a mood episode?
nodes.note: Schizoaffective requires a concurrent mood episode for the majority of the illness plus ≥2 weeks of psychosis without prominent mood symptoms. If mood episodes occupy only a minority, favor Schizophrenia; if psychosis is confined to mood episodes, favor a mood disorder with psychotic features.

no.outcome: Schizophrenia (mood episodes a minority of illness)

nodes.question: Has the disturbance lasted at least 1 month but less than 6 months?
Has the disturbance lasted at least 1 day but less than 1 month with return to premorbid functioning?
Are the delusion-like beliefs subthreshold or better explained by another disorder (e.g., OCD, body dysmorphic disorder, delusional-level)?

yes.outcome: Consider OCD/BDD with absent insight or another disorder

no.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorder

title: Hallucinations
overview: Distinguish true hallucinations from normal experiences (hypnagogic/hypnopompic phenomena, intense imagery) and illusions. The branching parallels the delusions tree: rule out substance and medical etiologies, then use the mood/psychosis relationship to differentiate the primary disorders. Hallucinations in clear consciousness confined to one modality, or occurring only at sleep-wake transitions, have distinct implications.

nodes.question: Do the hallucinations occur only while falling asleep or waking (hypnagogic/hypnopompic)?

yes.outcome: Normal sleep-related phenomena (consider narcolepsy if with cataplexy/other features)

nodes.question: Are the hallucinations due to the physiological effects of a substance (including medication or withdrawal)?
Are they due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition (including delirium)?

yes.outcome: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition / Delirium

diagnoses.name: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Do they occur exclusively during episodes of elevated/expansive/irritable mood?

diagnoses.name: Bipolar I/II Disorder, With Psychotic Features

nodes.question: Do they occur exclusively during Major Depressive Episodes?

diagnoses.name: Major Depressive Disorder, With Psychotic Features

nodes.question: Are the hallucinations part of a re-experiencing response to a traumatic event (flashbacks)?
Have psychotic symptoms persisted for 6 months or more?
Are they accompanied by other characteristic psychotic symptoms of schizophrenia?

no.outcome: Delusional Disorder (if delusions predominate) or reconsider

nodes.question: Is there a history of Major Depressive or Manic Episodes overlapping the active psychotic period?

no.outcome: Schizophrenia

nodes.question: Have mood episodes been present for the majority of the illness, with ≥2 weeks of psychosis without a mood episode?

no.outcome: Schizophrenia (mood a minority of illness)

nodes.question: Has the disturbance lasted at least 1 month but less than 6 months?
Has it lasted at least 1 day but less than 1 month with full recovery?

no.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Schizophrenia Spectrum and Other Psychotic Disorder

title: Catatonic Symptoms
presenting: Catatonic symptoms (stupor, mutism, posturing, rigidity, echophenomena, excitement)
overview: Catatonia is a syndrome, not a diagnosis. It occurs with medical conditions, psychotic disorders, and mood disorders, and it can be life-threatening (malignant catatonia). Identify the underlying context; DSM-5 codes catatonia as a specifier of another mental disorder, catatonia due to another medical condition, or unspecified catatonia.

nodes.question: Are the catatonic symptoms due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition?

yes.outcome: Catatonic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Catatonic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Are they due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (e.g., neuroleptic malignant syndrome, intoxication)?

yes.outcome: Substance/Medication-Induced (consider NMS as a medical emergency)

nodes.question: Do they occur in the context of a psychotic disorder (schizophrenia, schizophreniform, schizoaffective, brief psychotic)?

yes.outcome: Catatonia associated with a psychotic disorder

nodes.question: Do they occur in the context of a Manic or Major Depressive Episode?

yes.outcome: Catatonia associated with a mood disorder

nodes.question: Do they occur with the social-communication deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors of autism spectrum disorder?

yes.outcome: Catatonia associated with Autism Spectrum Disorder

nodes.question: Is the clinical picture a catatonia syndrome where the underlying disorder is not yet established?

no.outcome: Reconsider whether criteria for catatonia are met

title: Elevated or Expansive Mood
presenting: Elevated, expansive mood with increased energy/activity
overview: Establish whether the mood episode is a full Manic Episode (≥1 week or hospitalization, marked impairment/psychosis) or a Hypomanic Episode (≥4 days, observable but not markedly impairing, no psychosis). Manic and hypomanic episodes are the building blocks for the bipolar disorders. Always rule out substance/medication and medical causes first.

nodes.question: Is the mood disturbance due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (including antidepressant-triggered switch persisting beyond physiological effect)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition?

yes.outcome: Bipolar and Related Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Bipolar and Related Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Does the episode last ≥1 week (or require hospitalization) with marked impairment or psychotic features?
Manic Episode confirmed — is there any additional context that changes coding (e.g., psychotic features, mixed features)?

no.outcome: Bipolar I Disorder

nodes.question: Does the episode last ≥4 days with an observable, uncharacteristic change but without marked impairment or psychosis (Hypomanic Episode)?
Is there also a history of at least one Major Depressive Episode (and never a full Manic Episode)?

no.outcome: Other Specified Bipolar and Related Disorder (or reassess for prior mania/MDE)

diagnoses.name: Other Specified Bipolar and Related Disorder

nodes.question: Over ≥2 years, are there numerous periods of hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never meet full episode criteria?
Do elevated-mood symptoms occur but fall below threshold and cause clinically significant distress/impairment?

yes.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Bipolar and Related Disorder

diagnoses.name: Other Specified / Unspecified Bipolar and Related Disorder

no.outcome: Elevated mood not indicative of a bipolar disorder (e.g., normal happiness, temperament)

title: Irritable Mood
overview: Irritability is highly nonspecific and appears in mania, depression, anxiety, disruptive disorders, DMDD, personality disorders, PTSD, and as a normal reaction. Rule out substance/medical causes, then determine whether irritability marks a manic or depressive episode before considering the developmental and disruptive disorders.

nodes.question: Is the irritability due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition?

yes.outcome: Mental Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Does it occur during a period of elevated energy/activity meeting manic or hypomanic criteria?
Does it occur as part of a Major Depressive Episode or persistent depressive symptoms?
In a child ≤18 (onset before 10): severe recurrent temper outbursts with persistently irritable/angry mood between them, ≥12 months?
Does it occur with excessive anxiety/worry (e.g., generalized anxiety) or after trauma (PTSD)?
Is it part of a pattern of argumentative/defiant behavior (ODD) or recurrent aggressive outbursts (intermittent explosive disorder)?
Is it a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor?

no.outcome: Irritability not indicative of a mental disorder (temperament, situational)

title: Depressed Mood
overview: One of the most common presentations. After ruling out substance and medical etiologies, determine whether the depressed mood constitutes a Major Depressive Episode, then whether there is any history of mania/hypomania (which reclassifies the case as bipolar), and how psychotic symptoms relate to the mood episodes. Subthreshold, persistent, and stressor-related presentations are captured at the end.

nodes.question: Is the depressed mood due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition?

yes.outcome: Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is there ≥2 weeks of depressed mood and/or anhedonia with ≥5 total depressive symptoms (a Major Depressive Episode)?
Is there any lifetime history of a Manic or Hypomanic Episode?
nodes.note: A single lifetime manic/hypomanic episode reclassifies the case as bipolar.

nodes.question: Is there a history of delusions or hallucinations?

no.outcome: Major Depressive Disorder

nodes.question: Do the psychotic symptoms occur exclusively during Major Depressive Episodes?

yes.outcome: Major Depressive Disorder, With Psychotic Features

diagnoses.name: Major Depressive Disorder, With Psychotic Features

no.outcome: A Schizophrenia Spectrum / Other Psychotic Disorder is present

nodes.question: Is there depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for ≥2 years (≥1 year in children/adolescents)?
Do mood symptoms occur in the final premenstrual week and remit after menses, across most cycles?
Is the depressed mood a maladaptive response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor?
Are clinically significant depressive symptoms present but below threshold for the above?

no.outcome: Sadness not indicative of a mental disorder (e.g., ordinary sadness, uncomplicated grief)

title: Suicidal Ideation or Behavior
overview: Suicidal ideation and behavior cut across nearly every diagnostic grouping and demand immediate risk assessment independent of diagnosis. Diagnostically, identify the disorder(s) in which the ideation is occurring; treatment and safety planning take priority over nosology. This tree points to the disorders most commonly associated with suicidality.

nodes.question: Is the ideation/behavior occurring in the context of a substance intoxication/withdrawal state or medication effect?

yes.outcome: Address substance state; a substance-induced mood disorder may be present

nodes.question: Is it occurring during a Major Depressive Episode?
Is it occurring in the context of a psychotic disorder (e.g., command hallucinations, delusions)?
Is it occurring after a traumatic event with PTSD features?
Is the self-harm/ideation part of a pattern of affective instability, identity disturbance, and impulsivity?

yes.outcome: Borderline Personality Disorder (also see self-injury tree)

nodes.question: Is it a maladaptive response to a recent psychosocial stressor without another disorder?

no.outcome: Suicidal ideation/behavior not explained by a specific disorder — continue risk assessment and monitor

title: Psychomotor Retardation
overview: Slowing of movement and thought can reflect depression, catatonia, parkinsonism (including medication-induced), hypoactive delirium, neurocognitive disorders, and negative symptoms of psychosis. Rule out substance/medication (e.g., neuroleptics) and medical causes before attributing it to a primary mood or psychotic disorder.

nodes.question: Is it due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (e.g., sedatives, antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition (e.g., Parkinson's disease, hypothyroidism, hypoactive delirium)?

diagnoses.name: Delirium / Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Does it meet criteria for catatonia (with stupor, mutism, posturing, negativism)?
Does it occur as part of a Major Depressive or Manic Episode (mixed/with psychomotor changes)?
Does it occur as a negative symptom of a psychotic disorder?

no.outcome: Consider neurocognitive disorder or reassess — not attributable to a specific mood/psychotic disorder

title: Anxiety
overview: After ruling out substance and medical causes, the anxiety disorders are differentiated by the FOCUS of the fear/anxiety: separation from attachment figures, specific objects/situations, social scrutiny, unexpected panic and its consequences, or pervasive worry across domains. Obsessive-compulsive and trauma-related disorders are considered when the anxiety is tied to obsessions/compulsions or to a traumatic event.

nodes.question: Is the anxiety due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (e.g., caffeine, stimulants, withdrawal)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition (e.g., hyperthyroidism, arrhythmia)?

yes.outcome: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is the anxiety focused on separation from attachment figures?
Is it cued by a specific object or situation (e.g., heights, animals, injections)?
Is it focused on social situations involving possible scrutiny by others?
Are there recurrent unexpected panic attacks with persistent worry about further attacks or their consequences?
Is it focused on situations where escape may be difficult or help unavailable (e.g., public transport, open/enclosed spaces, crowds)?
Is it driven by obsessions and/or compulsions?
Does it follow exposure to a traumatic event with re-experiencing, avoidance, and hyperarousal?
Is there excessive worry about multiple events/activities, more days than not for ≥6 months, hard to control?
Is the anxiety a maladaptive response to an identifiable psychosocial stressor?
Are clinically significant anxiety symptoms present but below threshold for a specific disorder?

no.outcome: Anxiety within normal limits — not a mental disorder

title: Panic Attacks
overview: A panic attack is a symptom, not a disorder, and can occur in any anxiety disorder and many other conditions. The key distinction is between UNEXPECTED attacks (occurring without an obvious cue) and EXPECTED attacks (cued by a feared object/situation). Recurrent unexpected attacks plus anticipatory worry define panic disorder; expected attacks point to the disorder tied to their trigger.

nodes.question: Are the attacks due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (e.g., stimulant, caffeine, withdrawal)?
Are they due to the physiological effects of a general medical condition (e.g., arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma)?

yes.outcome: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Are the attacks cued exclusively by a specific phobic object/situation?
Are they cued exclusively by social scrutiny?
Are they cued exclusively by agoraphobic situations?
Are they cued exclusively by reminders of a traumatic event?
Are at least some attacks unexpected, with ≥1 month of worry about further attacks or maladaptive change in behavior?

no.outcome: Panic attacks present as a specifier of another disorder, or subthreshold — reassess the primary condition

title: Avoidance Behavior
overview: Avoidance is a final common pathway of many disorders; the diagnostic question is WHAT is being avoided and WHY. Identify the motivation for avoidance — feared objects, social scrutiny, panic-prone situations, trauma reminders, obsessional triggers, appearance concerns, or separation — to reach the underlying disorder.

nodes.question: Is the avoidance due to a substance/medication or general medical condition affecting the CNS?
Is avoidance driven by fear of specific objects/situations?
Is it driven by fear of social scrutiny/negative evaluation?
Is it driven by fear of panic-like symptoms in situations where escape is hard (agoraphobia)?
Is it avoidance of reminders of a traumatic event?
Is it avoidance triggered by obsessions (to prevent feared outcomes)?
Is it avoidance driven by perceived appearance flaws?
Is it avoidance of separation from attachment figures?
Is it a pervasive pattern of social inhibition and avoidance due to feelings of inadequacy and fear of criticism (personality-level)?

no.outcome: Avoidance not explained by a specific disorder — reassess motivation and context

title: Trauma or Psychosocial Stressors in the Etiology
presenting: Symptoms arising after a trauma or psychosocial stressor
overview: When symptoms follow an identifiable stressor, the differential turns on the nature of the stressor (traumatic vs. ordinary), the symptom profile, and timing/duration. Traumatic stressors with characteristic re-experiencing, avoidance, cognition/mood changes, and hyperarousal point to PTSD or acute stress disorder; a broader maladaptive response to a non-traumatic stressor suggests adjustment disorder. Other disorders can also be precipitated by stress.

nodes.question: Was the stressor an exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence (a traumatic stressor)?
Are there characteristic symptoms — intrusion/re-experiencing, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition/mood, and arousal?
Has the full symptom picture persisted for more than 1 month?

no.outcome: Acute Stress Disorder (3 days to 1 month)

nodes.question: Are there prominent dissociative symptoms (amnesia, depersonalization/derealization) related to the trauma?
In a child with pathogenic care, is there a pattern of inhibited/emotionally withdrawn behavior (or indiscriminate social behavior)?

yes.outcome: Reactive Attachment Disorder or Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder

diagnoses.name: Reactive Attachment Disorder / Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder

nodes.question: Do full criteria for another disorder (e.g., major depressive, anxiety, psychotic) precipitated by the stressor apply?
Are there clinically significant emotional/behavioral symptoms within 3 months of a stressor, in excess of expectation, not meeting another disorder?

no.outcome: Normal stress reaction / not a mental disorder

title: Somatic Complaints or Illness/Appearance Anxiety
overview: First ensure a general medical condition has been appropriately evaluated. The somatic symptom and related disorders are differentiated by whether distressing somatic symptoms are present, whether the focus is on having/acquiring a serious illness versus the symptoms themselves, whether there is deceptive symptom production, and whether neurological symptoms are incompatible with recognized disease.

nodes.question: Are the symptoms fully explained by a general medical condition (with a proportionate response)?

yes.outcome: General medical condition (consider Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions if psychological factors adversely affect it)

diagnoses.name: Psychological Factors Affecting Other Medical Conditions

nodes.question: Are symptoms intentionally produced/feigned for external incentives (malingering) or to assume the sick role (factitious)?

yes.outcome: Malingering (external incentive) or Factitious Disorder (no external incentive)

nodes.question: Are there neurological symptoms (weakness, movement, sensory, seizures) clinically incompatible with recognized disease?
Are there ≥1 distressing somatic symptoms with excessive thoughts/feelings/behaviors about them?
Is there preoccupation with having/acquiring a serious illness, with minimal or no somatic symptoms and high health anxiety?
Is there preoccupation with a perceived defect/flaw in physical appearance, with repetitive behaviors?
Are the somatic complaints better explained by a depressive, anxiety, or panic disorder?

no.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Somatic Symptom and Related Disorder, or no disorder

title: Appetite Changes or Unusual Eating Behavior
presenting: Appetite change or unusual eating behavior
overview: Distinguish appetite/weight change occurring as part of another disorder (depression, mania, anxiety, psychosis) or a medical/substance cause from the primary feeding and eating disorders, which are differentiated by restriction and low weight (anorexia), binge-purge cycles (bulimia), binge eating without compensation (binge-eating disorder), avoidant/restrictive intake without body-image disturbance (ARFID), and eating of nonnutritive substances (pica) or regurgitation (rumination).

nodes.question: Is the appetite/eating change due to a substance/medication or general medical condition?
Does it occur exclusively as part of a mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder?
Is there restriction of intake leading to significantly low body weight, fear of weight gain, and body-image disturbance?
Are there recurrent binges with compensatory behaviors (vomiting, laxatives, fasting, exercise), self-evaluation unduly influenced by shape/weight, at normal-ish weight?
Are there recurrent binges with marked distress but WITHOUT regular compensatory behavior?
Is there avoidance/restriction of food (based on sensory features or aversive consequences) with nutritional/psychosocial impact but no body-image disturbance?
Is there persistent eating of nonnutritive substances (pica) or repeated regurgitation (rumination)?

no.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Feeding or Eating Disorder, or no disorder

title: Insomnia
overview: Determine whether insomnia is due to a substance/medication, another sleep-wake disorder (e.g., a breathing-related or circadian disorder), or a coexisting mental disorder, or whether it is a persistent, independent insomnia disorder. DSM-5 allows insomnia disorder to be diagnosed alongside comorbid conditions when it is an independent focus of treatment.

nodes.question: Is the insomnia due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (including caffeine, withdrawal)?
Is it explained by another sleep-wake disorder (e.g., breathing-related, circadian rhythm, restless legs)?

diagnoses.name: Breathing-Related / Circadian Rhythm / Restless Legs / other sleep disorder

nodes.question: Is it due to another medical condition (e.g., pain, nocturia)?

yes.outcome: Insomnia related to another medical condition

diagnoses.name: Sleep disturbance due to another medical condition

nodes.question: Does the insomnia occur only during and is fully accounted for by another mental disorder (e.g., MDD, GAD)?

yes.outcome: Sleep disturbance as a feature of the underlying disorder

diagnoses.name: Major Depressive Disorder / Generalized Anxiety Disorder

nodes.question: Is there dissatisfaction with sleep quantity/quality ≥3 nights/week for ≥3 months with daytime impairment (independent focus)?

no.outcome: Situational/transient sleep difficulty — not a disorder

title: Hypersomnolence
overview: Excessive daytime sleepiness can arise from insufficient sleep, substances, other sleep disorders (notably narcolepsy and breathing-related sleep disorder), medical conditions, and mood disorders. Cataplexy, sleep paralysis, and hypnagogic hallucinations point specifically to narcolepsy.

nodes.question: Is the hypersomnolence due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication?
Is there cataplexy and/or evidence of hypocretin deficiency / characteristic REM findings?
Is it explained by a breathing-related sleep disorder (e.g., obstructive sleep apnea) or another sleep disorder?

yes.outcome: Breathing-Related Sleep Disorder / other sleep disorder

nodes.question: Is it due to another medical condition?

yes.outcome: Hypersomnolence due to another medical condition

diagnoses.name: Sleep disturbance due to another medical condition

nodes.question: Does it occur exclusively as part of another mental disorder (e.g., a Major Depressive Episode with hypersomnia)?

yes.outcome: Feature of the underlying mood disorder

nodes.question: Is there self-reported excessive sleepiness despite ≥7 hours sleep, ≥3 times/week for ≥3 months, with impairment (independent focus)?

no.outcome: Sleepiness due to insufficient sleep or situational factors — not a disorder

title: Sexual Dysfunction in a Female
overview: Sexual dysfunctions require clinically significant distress and typically ≥6 months' duration. Exclude substance/medication effects, medical conditions, severe relationship distress, and other mental disorders that better account for the problem before diagnosing a primary sexual dysfunction, which is then specified by the phase/nature of the difficulty.

nodes.question: Is the dysfunction due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (e.g., SSRIs)?
Is it fully explained by a general medical condition?

yes.outcome: Sexual dysfunction due to another medical condition (coded medically)

diagnoses.name: Sexual dysfunction attributable to a medical condition

nodes.question: Is it better explained by another mental disorder (e.g., major depressive disorder) or by severe relationship distress/other stressors?

yes.outcome: Diagnose the underlying disorder / note the stressor

nodes.question: Is there reduced/absent sexual interest and arousal?
Is there marked delay/absence/reduced intensity of orgasm?
Is there marked pain, tension, or fear with vaginal penetration?

no.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Sexual Dysfunction, or no disorder (if not distressing)

title: Sexual Dysfunction in a Male
overview: As with female sexual dysfunctions, require clinically significant distress and typically ≥6 months' duration, and exclude substance/medication effects, medical conditions, severe relationship distress, and other mental disorders before diagnosing a primary male sexual dysfunction, specified by desire, arousal/erectile, or ejaculatory phase.

nodes.question: Is the dysfunction due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication?
Is it fully explained by a general medical condition (e.g., vascular, neurologic, endocrine)?

yes.outcome: Sexual dysfunction due to another medical condition

diagnoses.name: Sexual dysfunction attributable to a medical condition

nodes.question: Is it better explained by another mental disorder or severe relationship distress?

yes.outcome: Diagnose the underlying disorder / note the stressor

nodes.question: Is there persistently deficient sexual/erotic thoughts and desire?
Is there difficulty obtaining/maintaining an erection or reduced erectile rigidity?
Is there ejaculation occurring sooner than desired (premature) or marked delay/absence (delayed)?

no.outcome: Other Specified / Unspecified Sexual Dysfunction, or no disorder (if not distressing)

title: Aggressive Behavior
overview: Aggression is nonspecific. Rule out substance intoxication/withdrawal and medical causes (including delirium and neurocognitive disorders), then determine whether aggression is a feature of a mood, psychotic, developmental, trauma, or personality disorder, or a discrete impulse-control problem (intermittent explosive disorder, conduct disorder). Some aggression is purposeful and not a disorder.

nodes.question: Is the aggression due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (intoxication/withdrawal)?
Is it due to a general medical condition (including delirium, neurocognitive disorder, personality change)?

diagnoses.name: Delirium / Neurocognitive Disorder / Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Does it occur only during manic or psychotic episodes?
In youth: severe recurrent temper outbursts with persistent irritability between them (DMDD)?
Does it follow trauma with PTSD-associated irritability/aggression?
Are there recurrent impulsive aggressive outbursts grossly out of proportion to provocation, not premeditated?
Is it part of a repetitive pattern of violating others' rights/norms (with a callous style)?

yes.outcome: Conduct Disorder (youth) or Antisocial Personality Disorder (adult)

nodes.question: Is it part of affective instability and impulsivity of borderline personality disorder?

no.outcome: Purposeful/instrumental aggression or reaction not attributable to a mental disorder

title: Impulsivity or Impulse-Control Problems
overview: Impulsivity appears across mania, ADHD, substance use, personality disorders, and the discrete impulse-control disorders (each defined by the specific impulsive behavior). Rule out substance/medical causes and episodic mood states, then match the behavior to its disorder (stealing → kleptomania, fire setting → pyromania, gambling → gambling disorder, hair pulling → trichotillomania, skin picking → excoriation).

nodes.question: Is the impulsivity due to a substance/medication or general medical condition?
Does it occur only during manic/hypomanic episodes?
Is there a persistent, cross-situational pattern of impulsivity with inattention/hyperactivity from childhood (ADHD)?
Is the specific behavior recurrent stealing of unneeded objects?
Is it deliberate fire setting with arousal/fascination?
Is it persistent, recurrent problematic gambling?
Is it recurrent hair pulling or skin picking with attempts to stop?
Is impulsivity part of a pervasive personality pattern (borderline, antisocial)?

no.outcome: Impulsivity not attributable to a specific disorder — reassess context

title: Self-Injury or Self-Mutilation
overview: Non-suicidal self-injury must be distinguished from suicidal behavior (see the suicidal ideation tree) and understood in its diagnostic context. Self-injury occurs with borderline personality disorder, in response to command hallucinations or delusions, in the context of stereotypies (intellectual disability, autism), and as a stress-related behavior. Always assess suicide risk in parallel.

nodes.question: Is the self-injury intended to end one's life (suicidal)?

diagnoses.name: See Suicidal Ideation or Behavior tree

nodes.question: Is it driven by psychotic symptoms (command hallucinations, delusions)?
Is it due to a substance/medication or general medical condition?
Is it repetitive, non-functional stereotyped self-injury with intellectual disability or autism?

yes.outcome: Stereotypic Movement Disorder, With Self-Injurious Behavior

nodes.question: Does it occur in a pattern of affective instability, identity disturbance, and impulsivity?
Is it recurrent intentional self-injury to relieve negative feelings, without suicidal intent, and not better explained above?

yes.outcome: Non-Suicidal Self-Injury (condition for further study / Other Specified)

no.outcome: Reassess motivation and context

title: Excessive Substance Use
overview: Two questions run in parallel: is there a substance use disorder (a maladaptive pattern with impaired control, social impairment, risky use, and pharmacological features), and are there substance-induced mental disorders (intoxication, withdrawal, or a substance-induced disorder such as psychotic, mood, or anxiety disorder)? This tree also anchors the substance-etiology decisions used throughout the other trees.

nodes.question: Is there a problematic pattern of use with ≥2 of: impaired control, social impairment, risky use, tolerance/withdrawal, within 12 months?

yes.outcome: Substance Use Disorder (specify substance and severity)

nodes.question: Are there reversible substance-specific symptoms from recent ingestion (intoxication)?
Are there substance-specific symptoms from cessation/reduction after heavy prolonged use (withdrawal)?
Are there prominent psychiatric symptoms (psychosis, mood, anxiety, sleep, sexual, cognitive) attributable to the substance and exceeding those expected of intoxication/withdrawal?
Is the excessive use non-substance (behavioral), specifically persistent problematic gambling?

no.outcome: Use present but not meeting disorder criteria — monitor / hazardous use (may warrant a Z code)

title: Memory Loss
overview: Distinguish amnesia due to a medical condition (including delirium and neurocognitive disorders) or a substance from dissociative amnesia (psychogenic, often for autobiographical/traumatic information, without a neurological basis) and from normal age-related forgetfulness. The presence/absence of other cognitive deficits, level of consciousness, and the nature of the forgotten material guide the differential.

nodes.question: Is the memory loss accompanied by a fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness (delirium)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication (e.g., alcohol blackout, benzodiazepines)?
Is it due to another medical condition, and accompanied by decline in memory (± other cognitive domains)?

yes.outcome: Major or Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is there an inability to recall important autobiographical information (often stressful/traumatic), too extensive for ordinary forgetting, without a neurological cause?
Does the memory complaint occur only during a mood, anxiety, or psychotic disorder (e.g., poor concentration in depression)?

no.outcome: Age-related or normal forgetfulness — not a mental disorder

title: Cognitive Impairment
presenting: Cognitive impairment (deficits in one or more cognitive domains)
overview: Broad cognitive impairment requires separating delirium (acute, fluctuating, with attentional disturbance) from the neurocognitive disorders (acquired decline from a prior level), intellectual disability (onset in the developmental period), and cognitive complaints that are features of other mental disorders (e.g., pseudodementia of depression). Establish onset, course, and whether consciousness is clear.

nodes.question: Is there an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness developing over hours to days (delirium)?
Is it due to the physiological effects of a substance/medication?
Do the deficits reflect intellectual and adaptive deficits with onset during the developmental period (not a decline)?
Is there acquired decline from a previous level in ≥1 cognitive domain (memory, executive, attention, language, perceptual-motor, social cognition)?
Do the deficits interfere with independence in everyday activities (vs. preserved independence with greater effort)?

no.outcome: Mild Neurocognitive Disorder

nodes.question: Are the cognitive complaints occurring only during another mental disorder (e.g., depression, psychosis)?

yes.outcome: Cognitive symptoms as a feature of the underlying disorder

no.outcome: No neurocognitive disorder — reassess or monitor

title: Etiological Medical Conditions
presenting: Psychiatric symptoms possibly due to another medical condition
overview: When a general medical condition is judged to physiologically cause the psychiatric symptoms, DSM-5 provides a family of 'Due to Another Medical Condition' diagnoses selected by the predominant symptom. This tree routes an established medical etiology to the correct disorder by presenting symptom.

nodes.question: Is there a fluctuating disturbance of attention/awareness with acute onset (delirium)?

yes.outcome: Delirium Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is there acquired cognitive decline (major/mild)?

yes.outcome: Major or Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Are psychotic symptoms (delusions/hallucinations) predominant?

yes.outcome: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Psychotic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is elevated/expansive/irritable mood with increased energy predominant?

yes.outcome: Bipolar and Related Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Bipolar and Related Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is depressed mood or anhedonia predominant?

yes.outcome: Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Depressive Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is anxiety (panic/worry) predominant?

yes.outcome: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Anxiety Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Are obsessive-compulsive/related symptoms predominant?

yes.outcome: Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: OCD and Related Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Is there a persistent personality change from baseline attributable to the medical condition?

yes.outcome: Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition

nodes.question: Are catatonic features predominant?

yes.outcome: Catatonic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

diagnoses.name: Catatonic Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition

no.outcome: If symptoms don't fit a specific category: Other Specified/Unspecified Mental Disorder Due to Another Medical Condition
